teaching.task: # HMS Year 12 V01 (Training for improved performance): pre-exercise screening. If exercise is good for almost everyone, why screen people before they start? (design)
teaching.causalExplanation: The puzzle goes away once you separate two kinds of risk. Across a whole population, regular activity lowers the risk of most chronic diseases. But for one person during a hard session, the heart rate, blood pressure and the heart's workload rise sharply, as you saw in Year 11. That briefly raises the risk of a serious event, and the extra risk sits almost entirely in people with heart disease they don't know about. Pre-exercise screening is a structured check to find that small group before they're asked to work hard. It does three jobs. Safety: spot conditions that make hard or unsupervised exercise unsafe right now. Duty of care: the legal and ethical duty to take reasonable steps to prevent harm you could foresee. And personalisation: the same answers describe the person's history, medicines, injuries and goals. So screening isn't there because exercise is dangerous. In Australia the standard tool is the APSS, the Adult Pre-Exercise Screening System. It has two stages. Stage 1 is compulsory for everyone. Questions one to six ask about known heart disease or stroke, unexplained chest pain, feeling faint or dizzy during activity, a recent asthma attack needing urgent care, trouble controlling diabetes, and any other condition needing special care. If all six are no, question seven asks how active you are, as weighted minutes: light and moderate minutes, plus twice the vigorous minutes, because a vigorous minute is about twice the work. Say a nineteen-year-old walks ninety minutes a week and plays thirty minutes of hard football. That's ninety plus sixty, a hundred and fifty. Below one fifty, the advice is light to moderate activity, built up gradually. At one fifty or more, continue at your current level. Stage 2 is recommended, done with an exercise professional, and reviews risk factors such as age, family history, smoking and blood pressure, to shape the program. Notice it doesn't sort people into fixed risk categories.

scenes.teachingReason: The puzzle goes away once you separate two kinds of risk. Across a whole population, regular activity lowers the risk of most chronic diseases. But for one person during a hard session, the heart rate, blood pressure and the heart's workload rise sharply, as you saw in Year 11. That briefly raises the risk of a serious event, and the extra risk sits almost entirely in people with heart disease they don't know about. Pre-exercise screening is a structured check to find that small group before they're asked to work hard. It does three jobs. Safety: spot conditions that make hard or unsupervised exercise unsafe right now. Duty of care: the legal and ethical duty to take reasonable steps to prevent harm you could foresee. And personalisation: the same answers describe the person's history, medicines, injuries and goals. So screening isn't there because exercise is dangerous.

scenes.teachingReason: In Australia the standard tool is the APSS, the Adult Pre-Exercise Screening System. It has two stages. Stage 1 is compulsory for everyone. Questions one to six ask about known heart disease or stroke, unexplained chest pain, feeling faint or dizzy during activity, a recent asthma attack needing urgent care, trouble controlling diabetes, and any other condition needing special care. If all six are no, question seven asks how active you are, as weighted minutes: light and moderate minutes, plus twice the vigorous minutes, because a vigorous minute is about twice the work. Say a nineteen-year-old walks ninety minutes a week and plays thirty minutes of hard football. That's ninety plus sixty, a hundred and fifty. Below one fifty, the advice is light to moderate activity, built up gradually. At one fifty or more, continue at your current level.

scenes.teachingReason: A screen only matters if someone acts on it. A yes to any of questions one to six means the person should get guidance from a doctor or an appropriate allied health professional before exercising. That isn't a diagnosis. It's about scope of practice, the limits of what a professional is trained and allowed to do. A personal trainer can't diagnose chest pain, so they make a referral, directing the person to someone who can. Stage 2 works differently. There's no automatic referral. scenes.teachingReason: Be precise about the limits too. A questionnaire is a filter, not a diagnosis. First, it relies on self-report. People may not know they have a condition, may forget, or may play down symptoms because they want to train. Second, it can't see disease with no symptoms, and that's exactly the group screening most wants to find. Third, it's a snapshot. Health changes, so people should be screened again at intervals, and after any injury, illness or pregnancy. So it's the first step, followed by watching during sessions and teaching people the warning signs.
